title: Red cells, then crackles
objective: Administer blood and blood products, recognize transfusion reactions (TRALI, TACO), and support plasmapheresis, exchange transfusion or leukocyte depletion

brief.situation: 21:00 in the PICU. You are the nurse for Maya, 6 years old, 20 kg, whose complete atrioventricular canal defect was repaired in infancy and who still has moderate valve regurgitation, on day 3 of an admission for pneumonia, and a hemoglobin of 6.8 g/dL. A unit of red cells started at 20:00 by pump; maintenance IV fluid is running alongside it.
handover: Her vital signs at 20:15 were normal and she had no reaction in the first 15 minutes.
At 20:55 she said she 'can't breathe right' and wants to sit up.

Unit transfusion policy: for any suspected reaction, stop the transfusion at once, keep the line open with saline through new tubing, check vital signs and the patient and product identity, call the intensivist and notify the blood bank, and return the bag and tubing; oxygen and upright positioning may be started by the nurse.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

then.log: New fine crackles at both bases, more on the right; she is using accessory muscles and prefers to sit up.
Heart rate up 25, blood pressure up 22 systolic, respiratory rate up 12, saturation down 5 points; temperature unchanged at 37.1.
Intake 640 mL including the red cells and maintenance fluid; output 120 mL. Neck veins full when upright; mild facial puffiness.
Name, record number and unit number match; ABO compatible.

why.question: What is happening to Maya during the transfusion, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: New respiratory distress within hours of a transfusion with crackles, hypertension, tachycardia, a positive fluid balance and a cardiac history, without fever or hives, is transfusion-associated circulatory overload.
parts.modelAnswer: She's in respiratory distress with crackles, her pressure and heart rate are up, she's 520 in, and she has a heart history. No fever or hives. That's circulatory overload from the transfusion.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Stops the transfusion and fluids at once, keeps the line open, sits her up with oxygen, gives no more volume, calls the intensivist and notifies the blood bank, and documents.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop the blood and the fluids, keep the line open, sit her up with oxygen, no more volume, call the intensivist and the blood bank, and document it.

edema.headline: Pulmonary edema, respiratory failure
edema.body: New respiratory distress with crackles, hypertension and a positive balance during a transfusion is circulatory overload. Stop the transfusion and fluids, sit her up with oxygen and call.

safe.headline: Overload recognized and treated
safe.body: You stopped the transfusion and fluids at once, sat her up with oxygen, gave no more volume and called the intensivist and blood bank within minutes. That is the expert path.

scoring.modelReasoning: TACO is new or worse respiratory distress, pulmonary edema, cardiovascular changes such as tachycardia, hypertension and a widened pulse pressure, and evidence of fluid overload within 12 hours of a transfusion. Maya has all of these and risk from her size and cardiac history. Stop the transfusion and the IV fluids at once, keep the line open, sit her up with oxygen, give no more volume, call the intensivist (who may order a diuretic) and notify the blood bank. Prevention next time: slower rates, split units and less crystalloid.
